questions.stem: A 72 year old woman is admitted with a urinary tract infection. Over 24 hours she becomes drowsy, her urine output falls to 15 mL per hour and she needs 6 L/min oxygen. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% on oxygen.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sepsis with failure of the renal, respiratory, cardiovascular and neurological systems is MODS; isolated delirium does not explain the oliguria and hypoxia.

clues: urine output falls to 15 mL per hour
steps.x: An infection followed by failure of kidneys, lungs, circulation and brain.

elim: Explains the infection but not failure of several organ systems.
No cardiac cause; the shock follows infection.
Several organ systems are already failing.
Would not explain oliguria and fever from a urinary source.

steps.x: C: Multi-organ dysfunction syndrome. Sepsis plus failure of two or more organ systems = MODS.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man is in intensive care with MODS from a perforated diverticulum. A student asks which combination of organ systems is most often involved in this syndrome. He is ventilated, on noradrenaline and his creatinine has doubled.
questions.q: Which group of organ systems is most commonly affected in this condition?
questions.e: The respiratory, renal and cardiovascular systems are the most commonly affected in MODS, as this man shows.

steps.x: Lungs, circulation and kidneys are all failing in this patient.

elim: Can be involved but are not the most common.
Less commonly the dominant failures.
Liver injury occurs but skin is not a classic organ failure.
Musculoskeletal failure is not a feature.

steps.x: E: Respiratory, renal and cardiovascular. Respiratory, renal and cardiovascular are the classic three.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man is reviewed on the surgical ward 2 days after an emergency bowel resection. He is newly confused, breathless and has passed 60 mL of urine in 6 hours. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 88/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on blood testing?
questions.e: Shock with failing organs produces anaerobic metabolism and a raised lactate, the key finding in MODS.

clues: passed 60 mL of urine in 6 hours
steps.x: Poor perfusion of several organs after surgery.

elim: Oliguria from acute kidney injury raises creatinine.
Urea rises with renal failure and hypovolaemia.
Lactic acidosis lowers the pH.
Albumin falls in critical illness.

steps.x: E: Raised serum lactate. Raised lactate marks poor tissue perfusion in MODS.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man is in intensive care 3 days after a crush injury to both legs in a building collapse. He has received 10 units of blood. He is now ventilated for hypoxia, needs noradrenaline and his creatinine has risen from 80 to 310 µmol/L. Blood cultures are negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: MODS can follow any severe systemic inflammatory response, including major trauma, not only sepsis.

steps.x: Major trauma, then lung, circulatory and renal failure without infection.

elim: Would not explain kidney and circulatory failure on its own.
Lungs and circulation are failing too.
Cultures are negative and the trigger is trauma, not infection.
Causes pulmonary oedema, not renal and vasopressor-dependent failure.

steps.x: C: Multi-organ dysfunction syndrome. Trauma can trigger MODS through systemic inflammation.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman with biliary sepsis is in intensive care. She is ventilated, on noradrenaline, receiving haemofiltration and her bilirubin is rising. Her daughter asks what most strongly predicts whether she will survive.
questions.q: Which factor most strongly determines her prognosis?
o: Number of organ systems that have failed
questions.e: Mortality rises sharply once two or more organ systems fail; she has four.

steps.x: Four organ systems are failing.

elim: Matters but less than organ failure count.
Does not track mortality closely.
Not a strong predictor.
Less important than the number of failed organs.

steps.x: B: Number of organ systems that have failed. The more organs fail, the higher the mortality.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man with pneumonia has been in intensive care for 48 hours on IV antibiotics, fluids and noradrenaline. Today his oxygen requirement has risen, his urine output has fallen further and his bilirubin has doubled.
questions.q: Which best describes his clinical course?
questions.e: Worsening organ function despite treatment, with a rising lactate, marks progression of MODS.

clues: for 48 hours on IV antibiotics, fluids and noradrenaline
steps.x: Organ function is getting worse despite full treatment.

elim: Does not explain worsening lungs and kidneys.
Organ function is worsening, not improving.
Would not explain rising bilirubin and lactate.
Rising lactate shows ongoing hypoperfusion.

steps.x: D: Progression of multi-organ dysfunction. Progression = worsening organ function despite treatment.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman with severe acute pancreatitis is reviewed on day 3. She is breathless with bilateral crackles, has had no urine for 6 hours and is confused. Her pulse rate is 130 bpm, BP 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88% on 10 L/min oxygen.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Systemic inflammatory response without organ failure
questions.e: Severe pancreatitis causes a systemic inflammatory response; respiratory, renal, cardiovascular and neurological failure together is MODS.

steps.x: Systemic inflammation from pancreatitis with several organs failing.

elim: No cardiac history; hypotension and oliguria follow pancreatitis.
Lungs, kidneys and circulation are all failing.
Confusion here is part of shock with other organ failures.
A late local complication, not systemic organ failure.

steps.x: C: Multi-organ dysfunction syndrome. Any severe inflammatory illness can cause MODS.

questions.stem: An 80 year old man has had cellulitis of his leg for 3 days. He is now confused with a falling urine output. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 86/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. His creatinine is 240 µmol/L and bilirubin 48 µmol/L.
questions.q: How is the diagnosis of his deterioration made?
o: Clinically, from evidence of dysfunction in two or more organs
questions.e: MODS is a clinical diagnosis based on evidence of dysfunction in two or more organ systems.

clues: confused with a falling urine output
creatinine is 240 µmol/L and bilirubin 48 µmol/L
steps.x: Brain, kidney, liver and circulation all show dysfunction.

elim: Identifies the cause but does not define organ failure.
Looks for a source, does not define the syndrome.
Not needed; dysfunction is shown by blood tests.
Excludes obstruction, does not make the diagnosis.

steps.x: B: Clinically, from evidence of dysfunction in two or more organs. MODS is diagnosed clinically from organ dysfunction.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman in intensive care with sepsis from an infected hip prosthesis develops acute kidney injury. Her fluid balance becomes 6 L positive and over the next day she needs intubation for worsening hypoxia with bilateral pulmonary infiltrates.
questions.q: Which best explains her respiratory deterioration?
o: Renal failure causing fluid overload that worsens lung function
questions.e: Organ failures interact: renal failure causes fluid overload which worsens respiratory failure, so mortality rises with each failed organ.

steps.x: Kidneys fail, fluid builds up, then lungs fail.

elim: No vomiting or reduced consciousness described.
No rash or anaphylaxis.
Gives a unilateral, not bilateral, picture.
Does not cause bilateral infiltrates after fluid overload.

steps.x: E: Renal failure causing fluid overload that worsens lung function. Organ failures feed each other in MODS.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man is admitted with an upper gastrointestinal bleed and has a cardiac arrest on the ward. After return of spontaneous circulation he remains on noradrenaline, his lactate is 9 mmol/L, his ALT is 2400 U/L and he is anuric.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Shock from haemorrhage and arrest caused failure of the circulation, liver and kidneys with a high lactate: MODS.

steps.x: Circulatory, liver and kidney failure after shock.

elim: No overdose; the liver injury follows hypoperfusion.
Needs established cirrhosis and occurs without shock.
Kidneys and circulation are also failing.
No crush or muscle injury described.

steps.x: D: Multi-organ dysfunction syndrome. Two or more failing organs after a major insult = MODS.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman with faecal peritonitis has received 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid and IV antibiotics. Her BP has risen from 82/50 to 104/62 mmHg. The team wants to know whether tissue perfusion is improving.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to monitor her response to resuscitation?
questions.e: Lactate reflects anaerobic metabolism from poor oxygen delivery, so its trend shows whether resuscitation is working.

clues: received 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid and IV antibiotics
steps.x: The question asks about perfusion after resuscitation.

elim: Identifies a source, not perfusion.
Does not measure perfusion.
Tracks infection, not perfusion.
Not a perfusion marker.

steps.x: C: Repeat serum lactate. Repeat lactate tracks response to resuscitation.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with MODS from pneumonia is breathless with a respiratory rate of 34 breaths per minute. His oxygen saturation is 89% on 15 L/min via a non-rebreather mask. The team needs to decide whether he needs ventilation.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: An arterial blood gas shows hypoxia, hypercapnia and acidosis, confirming respiratory involvement and guiding ventilation.

steps.x: Respiratory failure needs to be quantified.

elim: Not first; hypoxia must be quantified now.
Not useful in pneumonia with respiratory failure.
Cannot be done by an acutely breathless patient.
Identifies the organism but not the severity of respiratory failure.

steps.x: A: Arterial blood gas. ABG assesses respiratory involvement in MODS.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman becomes hypotensive, oliguric and jaundiced on the ward 5 days after a cholecystectomy. Her temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 120 bpm and BP 86/50 mmHg. Her lactate is 4.4 mmol/L. The source of her deterioration is not clear.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the cause, taken before antibiotics?
questions.e: Blood cultures, with imaging, identify the cause of MODS; she likely has a post-operative biliary infection.

clues: source of her deterioration is not clear
steps.x: Fever after surgery with organ failure: find the infection.

elim: Not relevant to acute septic deterioration.
Measures dysfunction, not the cause.
Pancreatitis is not suggested.
Will not identify an infective source.

steps.x: B: Blood cultures. Cultures and imaging identify the cause of MODS.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man with septic shock from cholangitis is reviewed in intensive care. He is jaundiced and his urine output is 10 mL per hour. The consultant asks which blood test best shows that his liver is now involved.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate test to assess liver dysfunction?
questions.e: Organ-specific markers in MODS: bilirubin for the liver, creatinine for the kidney and ABG for the lungs.

steps.x: The question names the liver.

elim: Tests the pancreas.
Tests the kidney, not the liver.
Tests the heart.
Shows inflammation, not liver function.

steps.x: B: Serum bilirubin. Bilirubin = liver marker in MODS.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman with septic shock from pneumonia has passed 50 mL of urine in 8 hours despite a noradrenaline infusion. Her BP is 104/60 mmHg on noradrenaline.
questions.q: Which result most strongly supports renal involvement?
questions.e: A raised creatinine with oliguria shows acute kidney injury; renal failure is one of the most common organ failures in MODS.

steps.x: Oliguria points at the kidney.

elim: Reflects the liver, not the kidney.
Reflects inflammation only.
Mild anaemia, not a renal marker.
Mild thrombocytopenia, not renal.

steps.x: B: Creatinine 312 µmol/L. Creatinine = renal marker in MODS.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man is admitted from the emergency department with a urinary source of sepsis. He is confused, his BP is 84/52 mmHg, urine output is 10 mL per hour and lactate 4.8 mmol/L. Blood cultures have been taken and IV fluids started.
questions.q: Which is the most important treatment to reverse his organ dysfunction?
questions.e: First-line treatment of MODS is treating the cause; here IV antibiotics for sepsis.

steps.x: The cause is sepsis.

elim: Only for refractory shock, not first-line.
Oral treatment is inadequate for septic shock.
No bleeding or low platelets.
Monitors output but does not treat the cause.

steps.x: A: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics. Treat the underlying cause: antibiotics for sepsis.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman with MODS from necrotising fasciitis is on a noradrenaline infusion and is ventilated. She has been anuric for 12 hours and her potassium is 6.9 mmol/L with a pH of 7.12 despite medical treatment.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Refractory hyperkalaemia and acidosis in anuric renal failure need dialysis as organ support.

steps.x: Renal failure with refractory acidosis and hyperkalaemia.

elim: Will not work in anuric AKI and does not correct acidosis.
Too slow and ineffective in a ventilated patient.
Not indicated in septic AKI.
Would worsen renal perfusion.

steps.x: D: Renal replacement therapy. Dialysis supports renal failure in MODS.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with MODS from pneumonia has received 30 mL/kg of IV crystalloid and IV antibiotics. His BP remains 78/44 mmHg, his lactate is 5.2 mmol/L and he is being transferred to intensive care.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Persistent hypotension despite fluid needs vasopressors (noradrenaline) in intensive care for cardiovascular failure.

steps.x: Fluid-refractory hypotension.

elim: Fluids alone have failed; more risks overload.
Not used in acute shock.
No bleeding or low haemoglobin.
Delays support of failing circulation.

steps.x: D: Vasopressor infusion. Vasopressors support cardiovascular failure.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man with motor neurone disease is admitted with aspiration pneumonia and develops MODS. He is alert, fully oriented and understands that intensive care would mean intubation. He clearly says he does not want to be ventilated.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Assess and document his decision-making capacity
Refer to the Court of Protection
questions.e: In serious illness the first step is to assess capacity; a capacitous patient can refuse escalation.

clues: clearly says he does not want to be ventilated
steps.x: An alert patient is refusing treatment.

elim: He may have capacity; the decision is his.
Overrides a possibly capacitous refusal.
Not needed unless capacity is disputed.
Ignores his stated wishes.

steps.x: B: Assess and document his decision-making capacity. Assess capacity before decisions about escalation.

questions.stem: An 88 year old woman with advanced dementia and frailty is in hospital with MODS from a perforated bowel despite antibiotics and fluids. She is unresponsive and has no advance decision or lasting power of attorney. Her three children are at the bedside.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Discuss escalation versus palliative care with her family
Intubate and transfer to intensive care
Wait for her to regain capacity
questions.e: When the patient lacks capacity, discuss escalation versus palliative care with family to reach an agreed, ethically and legally sound decision.

steps.x: She lacks capacity and has no attorney.

elim: Ignores her frailty and best interests.
Not decided without a best-interests discussion.
Must involve family in a best-interests decision.
She is unresponsive; decisions are needed now.

steps.x: A: Discuss escalation versus palliative care with her family. Lacks capacity: best-interests discussion with family.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man develops lung, kidney and liver failure 2 days after severe faecal peritonitis. A student asks what causes many distant organs to fail at once.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Direct bacterial invasion of each organ
Systemic inflammation causing microvascular dysfunction and poor perfusion
questions.e: A severe systemic inflammatory response causes microvascular dysfunction and reduced tissue perfusion, leading to progressive organ failure.

clues: many distant organs to fail at once
steps.x: Distant organs fail together.

elim: Not the mechanism of MODS.
Organs fail without being infected themselves.
Does not explain simultaneous multi-organ failure.
Would affect the lungs, not all organs.

steps.x: D: Systemic inflammation causing microvascular dysfunction and poor perfusion. Systemic inflammation, microvascular dysfunction, poor perfusion.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman with sepsis from a liver abscess is on noradrenaline in intensive care. Her mean arterial pressure is 75 mmHg, but her lactate keeps rising and her urine output remains low. Her daughter asks why her organs are failing when her blood pressure is now normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Cytokine-mediated endothelial damage impairing microcirculatory flow
questions.e: Cytokines damage endothelium so the microcirculation fails even when the macrocirculation (blood pressure) is restored.

steps.x: Normal BP, but organs still poorly perfused.

elim: Her pressure is normal, not high.
No reason to doubt the reading.
High output does not cause organ failure.
Not given and would not explain this.

steps.x: A: Cytokine-mediated endothelial damage impairing microcirculatory flow. Microcirculatory failure can occur despite normal BP.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man with MODS has a lactate of 6.2 mmol/L. After fluids and noradrenaline it falls to 2.4 mmol/L over 6 hours. A student asks why lactate rose in the first place.

visual.title: Lactate during resuscitation
visual.caption: Falling lactate shows tissue perfusion is improving.

questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the raised lactate?
o: Anaerobic metabolism from inadequate tissue oxygen delivery
questions.e: Poor oxygen delivery forces cells into anaerobic metabolism, producing lactate; its fall shows improving perfusion.

steps.x: Lactate fell when perfusion was restored.

elim: Would lower lactate.
Ketones are separate from lactate.
No metformin mentioned.
Thiamine deficiency, not excess, raises lactate.

steps.x: A: Anaerobic metabolism from inadequate tissue oxygen delivery. Raised lactate = anaerobic metabolism from poor oxygen delivery.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman in intensive care with sepsis develops cardiovascular failure on day 1, renal failure on day 2 and respiratory failure on day 3. Her predicted mortality has climbed steeply with each new failure.
questions.q: Which best explains why mortality rises so sharply with each additional failed organ?
o: Each organ fails from a different infection
Organ function is interconnected, so each failure worsens the others
The number of organs is unrelated to outcome
questions.e: Organ perfusion and function are interconnected, e.g. renal failure causes fluid overload that worsens respiratory failure.

steps.x: Failures appear one after another.

elim: Not the reason mortality rises.
There is one source.
Support does not drive the steep rise.
Contradicts the known sharp rise.

steps.x: D: Organ function is interconnected, so each failure worsens the others. Interconnected organs: one failure drives the next.
